If you can surrender to its crepuscular ebb and flow and wincing interrogation of masculinity then it will indeed thrill.
Mark Strong is brilliant in the role: a man initially so anodyne that he blends into his dull background, he gradually hardens before your eyes until his every move makes you jump.
Mark Strong moves from bland to bludgeoning as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Even his name, Donald Dodd, is on the dull side. His envy of other men and the things they have, the things they do, gets horribly tangled up in his attraction to Mona. Robert Icke, when on form, is a master of atmosphere and suspense.
Robert Icke directs the entire affair with a stern artfulness, making the dialogue deliberately pointed, the pace pointedly slow as he builds to a genuinely frightening climax.
Whodunit fans should heed my sincere praise for this show even though I spent much of it with my eyes clenched tight and both my ears plugged with gummy fingers.

This production is all about the scenery sliding in and out which it does very efficiently but considering the extensive high-tech, back stage facilities at the National Theatre even this feels unremarkable very quickly.
What might have been a claustrophobic three-hander is wrecked by Robert Icke's ludicrously overblown direction and some uneasy casting.

cn.t: Hare's adaptation of Simenon's noir novel divides critics. Some praise Icke's stylish direction and the psychological tension, while others find it a puzzling departure that prioritizes mood over thrills in this interval-free study of masculinity.
